title: The Integumentary System
description: Week 6: the layers of the skin, glands, hair and nails, skin functions, wound healing, burns, pressure injuries, skin disorders, transdermal medications, and the skin assessment.

heel.intro: A nurse is caring for a 74-year-old client on a medical-surgical unit, 3 days after surgery to repair a fractured right hip.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Nurses' Notes

Day 3, 0800:

Client is alert and oriented. Reports right hip pain of 6 on a scale of 0 to 10 and prefers to stay on the back, because turning hurts. Has eaten about one-quarter of each meal for 2 days and takes only small sips of water. Was incontinent of urine overnight; the sheets were damp at 0600. Skin over the sacrum is intact. Right heel: a 3 cm area of dark red skin that does not blanch when pressed; the skin is intact, with no blister. Left heel: intact, and the color matches the surrounding skin. Client has type 2 diabetes mellitus and reports decreased feeling in both feet.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the layers of the epidermis. Which layer contains the stem cells that divide to replace skin cells, along with the melanocytes that make melanin?
options: Stratum corneum
Stratum basale
Stratum lucidum
Stratum granulosum
questions.rationale:
The stratum basale (basal layer, also called the stratum germinativum) is the deepest layer of the epidermis, next to the dermis. It is mitotically active: its stem cells divide, and the new keratinocytes move upward to form the other layers. It also holds the melanocytes, which make melanin.

The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of flat, keratinized cells that limits water loss; its cells no longer divide. The stratum lucidum is a clear layer found only in the thick skin of the palms and soles. In the stratum granulosum, cells fill with lipid-rich granules and begin to lose their nuclei as they move away from the blood supply in the dermis.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the structure of the thick skin on the palm of the hand. Place the layers of the epidermis in order, from the deepest layer to the skin surface.
questions.rationale:
From deepest to surface: the stratum basale (dividing cells and melanocytes, next to the dermis), the stratum spinosum (several layers of keratinocytes held together by desmosomes, which look like spines), the stratum granulosum (cells with lipid-rich granules that begin to lose their nuclei), the stratum lucidum (a clear layer found only in the thick skin of the palms and soles), and the stratum corneum (the outer keratin layer that limits water loss).

Keratinocytes form in the basal layer and mature as they move outward. In skin other than the palms and soles, there is no stratum lucidum, so the granulosum lies directly under the corneum.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a cross-section of the skin. Click the layer that has no blood vessels of its own and is made mostly of keratinocytes.
questions.alt: Cross-section of the skin with the surface at the top: a thin top layer, a thicker middle layer with blood vessels, a nerve ending, a hair follicle, a gland beside the follicle, and a coiled gland, and a deep layer of fat cells above the muscle.
questions.rationale:
The epidermis, the thin top layer, is avascular: it has no blood vessels, so its cells get nutrients by diffusion from the dermis below. About 90% of its cells are keratinocytes, which form a barrier against heat, UV radiation, dehydration, and microorganisms.

The dermis, the thicker middle layer, is connective tissue rich in collagen, with blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles, and glands. The hypodermis (subcutaneous layer), the deep layer of fat, cushions the body, insulates it, stores energy, and anchors the skin to the tissues below.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the dermis. Which statements describe the dermis?
options: It is the outermost layer that limits water loss.
It contains blood vessels that nourish the epidermis.
It is connective tissue made mostly of collagen.
It is avascular and gets its nutrients by diffusion.
Hair follicles and sweat glands are found in it.
It contains nerve endings and mechanoreceptors.
questions.rationale:
The dermis is a connective tissue layer whose main component is collagen, which gives the skin strength and flexibility. Its blood vessels feed the epidermis and support the inflammatory response, it holds nerve endings and mechanoreceptors for sensation, and hair follicles and glands sit in it (sweat glands can reach down into the subcutaneous layer).

The outermost layer that limits water loss is the stratum corneum of the epidermis, not the dermis. The epidermis, not the dermis, is avascular and gets its nutrients by diffusion from the dermis.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to give a subcutaneous injection. Click the layer of tissue that the medication should reach.
questions.alt: Cross-section of the skin with the surface at the top: a thin top layer, a thicker middle layer with blood vessels, a nerve ending, a hair follicle, a gland beside the follicle, and a coiled gland, and a deep layer of fat cells above the muscle.
questions.rationale:
A subcutaneous injection goes into the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer), the deep layer of loose connective tissue and fat between the dermis and the muscle. Besides holding injected medication, this layer cushions the body, stores energy, insulates, and anchors the skin to the structures below.

The epidermis (top layer) and the dermis (middle layer, with blood vessels, glands, and hair follicles) are not the target of a subcutaneous injection; an intradermal injection is placed just under the epidermis. The muscle below the fat is the target of an intramuscular injection.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the cells of the epidermis. What is the role of Langerhans cells?
options: They produce melanin, which absorbs ultraviolet light.
They make the keratin that forms the skin's protective barrier.
They take up microbial antigens and present them to the immune system.
They detect high-frequency vibration and deep pressure.
questions.rationale:
Langerhans cells are immune cells that live in the epidermis (most prominent in the stratum spinosum) and act like macrophages. In a skin infection, they take up microbial antigens and become antigen-presenting cells, starting the immune response.

Melanocytes, in the stratum basale, produce melanin, which absorbs most UV light. Keratinocytes, about 90% of epidermal cells, make keratin and form the barrier. Pacinian corpuscles, in the deep dermis, sense high-frequency vibration and deep pressure.

questions.stem: A client asks a nurse what makes the skin and scalp oily. Click the gland that secretes sebum.
questions.alt: Cross-section of the skin with the surface at the top: a thin top layer, a thicker middle layer with blood vessels, a nerve ending, a hair follicle, a gland beside the follicle, and a coiled gland, and a deep layer of fat cells above the muscle.
questions.rationale:
The sebaceous gland sits beside the hair follicle. Together with the hair, the follicle, and the arrector pili muscle, it forms the pilosebaceous unit. It secretes sebum, a mixture of lipids that forms a thin film on the skin and hair, helps prevent fluid loss, and has an antimicrobial role.

The coiled gland deeper in the dermis is an eccrine sweat gland, which makes watery sweat that cools the body as it evaporates. The hair follicle holds the hair, and the fat cells below belong to the subcutaneous layer.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the glands of the skin. For each description, click to specify the gland it describes.
rows: Produces earwax in the ear canal
Secretes oily sebum into the hair follicle
Found in the axillae and genital area; its secretions cause body odor when bacteria break them down
Releases watery sweat over most of the body to cool it by evaporation
questions.rationale: Eccrine sweat glands are found throughout the body and produce watery (serous) sweat that cools the body as it evaporates. Apocrine glands are concentrated in the axillae, areolae, and genital area and release a thicker, protein-rich sweat; body odor comes from bacteria breaking it down. Sebaceous glands, part of the pilosebaceous unit, secrete sebum into the hair follicle. Ceruminous glands, modified apocrine glands in the ear canal, produce cerumen (earwax).

questions.stem: During a skin assessment, a nurse notes that a client's fingernails curve upward at the ends, like a spoon. The nurse should ask the client about a history of which condition?
options: Iron deficiency anemia
Psoriasis
Chronic lung disease
A fungal nail infection
questions.rationale:
Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), in which the outer edge of the nail curves upward, are associated with iron deficiency anemia, though they can also occur without a known cause.

Psoriasis is associated with pitting, small pits in the nail plate. Chronic lung disease is associated with clubbing, a flattened angle between the nail and the nail fold. A fungal infection (onychomycosis) causes discolored, thickened nails with debris under the nail and splitting.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing the fingers of a client who has cystic fibrosis. Which finding indicates clubbing?
options: Small, deep pits are scattered across the surface of the nail plates.
The angle at the nail base is flattened, and the fingertip is enlarged.
The nails curve upward at the ends, so they look like a spoon.
The nails are thick and yellow, with crumbly debris under them.
questions.rationale:
Clubbing is an increased curve and thickening of the fingertip with flattening (loss) of the angle between the nail plate and the nail fold, best seen from the side. It is associated with chronic lung and heart disease, including cystic fibrosis, lung cancer, and interstitial lung disease, and calls for a full assessment of oxygenation.

Pitting occurs with psoriasis, eczema, and alopecia areata. Spoon nails (koilonychia) are associated with iron deficiency anemia. Thick, yellow nails with debris suggest a fungal infection (onychomycosis).

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of clients about hair loss. Which statements are accurate?
options: Scarring alopecia destroys the hair follicles, so the hair loss is permanent.
Alopecia areata always leaves permanent bald patches.
Telogen effluvium can follow severe stress, illness, or childbirth.
Alopecia areata is an immune-mediated hair loss, and the hair may grow back.
Male pattern baldness is inherited and depends on androgens.
Folliculitis is most often caused by a virus.
questions.rationale:
Alopecia areata is a chronic, immune-mediated, nonscarring hair loss, most often in patches on the scalp; it can go away on its own, with the hair growing back. In scarring alopecia, the follicles are destroyed, so the loss is permanent. Male pattern (androgenetic) baldness is inherited and androgen-dependent: dihydrotestosterone shortens the growth phase of the follicles. Telogen effluvium is a nonscarring shedding that can follow psychological stress, severe or chronic illness, pregnancy and childbirth, surgery, or some medications.

Folliculitis, an inflammation of the hair follicle with pustules and red papules, is most often bacterial (usually Staphylococcus aureus), not viral. Because alopecia areata is nonscarring, its bald patches are not always permanent.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the sensory receptors of the skin. For each receptor, click to specify what it senses.
columns: Light touch and movement across the skin
rows: Pacinian corpuscle
Meissner corpuscle
Ruffini ending
Merkel cell
Free nerve ending
questions.rationale: Pacinian corpuscles, large layered receptors in the deep dermis, sense high-frequency vibration and deep pressure. Meissner corpuscles, in the dermal papillae of hairless skin such as the fingertips, sense light touch and movement across the skin. Ruffini endings sense stretch. Merkel cells sense steady pressure, edges, and shapes, which helps the brain build a picture of what is touched. Free nerve endings in the epidermis detect pain and temperature.

questions.stem: A client is working outdoors on a hot day. Which response of the skin helps the client's body lose heat?
options: Constriction of the blood vessels in the dermis
Dilation of the blood vessels in the dermis
Contraction of the arrector pili muscles
Shivering of the skeletal muscles
questions.rationale:
When the body is warm, the hypothalamus triggers vasodilation of the dermal blood vessels, which brings more warm blood near the surface so heat can leave the body, and the eccrine glands make sweat that cools the skin as it evaporates.

Vasoconstriction keeps warm blood away from the surface to conserve heat in the cold. Contraction of the arrector pili muscles makes the hairs stand up, which traps a layer of warm air near the skin. Shivering is muscle activity that produces heat. All three help keep heat in, not let it out.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching how the body makes active vitamin D. Place the steps in order.
items: Ultraviolet B light from the sun reaches the skin.
7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin changes to previtamin D.
Heat converts previtamin D to vitamin D3.
The liver converts vitamin D3 to 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
The kidneys convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
questions.rationale: Vitamin D synthesis starts when ultraviolet B light (290 to 315 nm) reaches the skin and changes 7-dehydrocholesterol into previtamin D. Body heat then converts previtamin D into vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol). Vitamin D from the skin and the diet goes to the liver, which makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and then to the kidneys, which make the active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). The last step is regulated by parathyroid hormone, calcium, and phosphorus.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for an older adult who is homebound and rarely goes outdoors. The nurse explains that sunlight on the skin helps the body make vitamin D. Which function of vitamin D should the nurse include in the teaching?
options: It stimulates the melanocytes to produce more melanin.
It forms the collagen that strengthens the dermis.
It controls how much the client sweats in hot weather.
It helps the intestine absorb calcium for healthy bones.
questions.rationale:
The active form of vitamin D (calcitriol) increases calcium absorption from the intestine, which is essential for bone health. A client who gets little sun depends on vitamin D from the diet, and may need it checked or supplemented as the provider prescribes.

Vitamin D does not make melanin (melanocytes make it from tyrosine), does not form collagen (fibroblasts do), and does not control sweating (the sympathetic nervous system does).

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how sweating is controlled. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: Sweat glands are stimulated by the {{0}} nervous system. Sweating far beyond what the body needs to control its temperature is called {{1}}.

options: parasympathetic
sympathetic
somatic
seborrhea
hypothermia
hyperhidrosis

questions.rationale:
Sweat glands are stimulated by the sympathetic nervous system, through cholinergic autonomic neurons. In hyperhidrosis, an abnormal central response to normal emotional stress increases sympathetic signaling, so the eccrine glands make more sweat than temperature control requires.

The parasympathetic system does not control sweating, and the somatic nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle. Seborrhea refers to excess oil and scaling, as in seborrheic dermatitis, and hypothermia is a low core body temperature.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client who has dark skin for cyanosis. Where should the nurse look?
options: The lips and oral mucosa
The skin of the forearm
The skin of the abdomen
The skin of the back
questions.rationale:
Cyanosis is easiest to see where the skin or membrane is thin and the blood supply is rich, such as the lips and oral mucosa, nose, cheeks, ears, and nail beds. In clients with darker skin, the mucous membranes and nail beds are especially important, because pigment can hide color changes in the skin itself. Good lighting matters too.

The skin of the forearm, abdomen, and back is thicker and more pigmented, with less superficial blood flow, so cyanosis can be missed there.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who has liver disease and a rising bilirubin level. Where does jaundice usually appear first?
options: The palms of the hands
The nail beds
The lips
The sclera of the eyes
questions.rationale:
Jaundice (hyperbilirubinemia) is a yellow color from bilirubin building up in the tissues. It usually shows first in the sclera (scleral icterus), once the serum bilirubin rises above about 3 mg/dL (normal is less than 1 mg/dL). The sclera is especially useful to check in clients with darker skin.

The palms, nail beds, and lips are not where jaundice first appears. The nail beds and lips are better places to look for cyanosis or pallor.

questions.stem: A nurse is performing a skin assessment. Which findings can point to a disease in another body system?
options: Warm, dry skin in a comfortable room
Yellow sclera
Clubbing of the fingernails
Dark, velvety patches on the back of the neck
Bluish lips and nail beds
A small mole that has looked the same for years
questions.rationale:
The skin often reflects disease elsewhere. Yellow sclera (jaundice) suggests liver dysfunction. Clubbing is associated with chronic lung and heart disease. Bluish lips and nail beds (cyanosis) suggest low oxygen, as in COPD, pneumonia, or pulmonary edema. Dark, velvety patches in skin folds such as the back of the neck (acanthosis nigricans) are associated with insulin resistance and diabetes.

A mole that hasn't changed for years is not a warning sign; change (evolving) is one of the warning signs of melanoma. Warm, dry skin in a comfortable room is a normal finding.

questions.stem: A student asks a nurse why people have different skin tones. Which explanation is accurate?
options: People with darker skin have many more melanocytes in the epidermis.
Darker skin has a thicker stratum corneum that blocks more light.
Lighter skin has fewer blood vessels in the dermis, so it looks paler.
The amount and spread of melanin differ, not the number of melanocytes.
questions.rationale:
People of all skin tones have roughly the same number of melanocytes. Skin tone depends on how much melanin the melanocytes make, and on the size and density of the melanin they pass to the keratinocytes. Melanin protects the cells' DNA from UV radiation.

Darker skin does not have more melanocytes. Skin tone does not come from a thicker stratum corneum or from the number of blood vessels, although blood flow and oxygenation do change skin color (redness, pallor, cyanosis).

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client how a surgical incision heals. Place the phases of wound healing in order.
questions.rationale: Healing begins with hemostasis: vessels constrict, platelets clump, and the coagulation cascade forms a fibrin clot. In the inflammatory phase, neutrophils and monocytes move in to destroy bacteria and clear debris. In the proliferative phase (by about days 5 to 7), fibroblasts lay down new collagen, granulation tissue fills the wound, new blood vessels grow, and new epithelium covers the surface. The maturation (remodeling) phase starts around week 3 and can last up to 12 months, as excess collagen is broken down and the scar gains strength.

questions.stem: For each event, click to specify the phase of wound healing in which it occurs.
rows: Excess collagen breaks down, and the scar gains strength over months
Platelets clump and a fibrin clot forms
Neutrophils and monocytes destroy bacteria and clear debris
Fibroblasts lay down new collagen, and granulation tissue forms
questions.rationale: In hemostasis, right after the injury, platelets clump and the coagulation cascade forms a fibrin clot. In the inflammatory phase, neutrophils and monocytes move in to destroy bacteria and clear debris. In the proliferative phase (by about days 5 to 7), fibroblasts lay down new collagen and granulation tissue fills the wound. In maturation (remodeling), from about week 3 for up to 12 months, excess collagen is broken down and the scar slowly strengthens.

questions.stem: A client who had abdominal surgery 4 weeks ago asks whether the incision is now as strong as the skin was before surgery. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: It regained its full strength by the end of the first week after surgery.
Once it's fully healed, the scar will be stronger than the skin was before.
Healing is complete now that the incision is closed and the stitches are out.
It keeps getting stronger for months, but only to about 80% of the original.
questions.rationale:
The maturation (remodeling) phase begins around week 3 and can last up to 12 months. Wound strength peaks at about 11 to 14 weeks, but a scar never regains all of the original strength: it reaches only about 80%.

At the end of the first week, the wound is still in the proliferative phase, with new collagen just being laid down. A scar is not stronger than the original skin. Closure of the skin does not mean healing is complete, because remodeling continues for months.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing factors that affect wound healing. Which factors can delay healing?
options: Smoking
Advanced age
Poor nutrition
Good circulation to the area
Diabetes mellitus
Adequate protein intake
Wound infection
questions.rationale:
Diabetes impairs circulation and the immune response. Smoking constricts blood vessels and reduces oxygen delivery. Poor nutrition deprives the wound of the protein and nutrients it needs to build new tissue. Infection prolongs inflammation and destroys new tissue. Advanced age slows cell turnover and healing.

Good circulation and adequate protein intake promote healing, because they bring oxygen and the building blocks of new collagen to the wound.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a surgical wound that was left open to heal by secondary intention 6 days ago. Which finding shows that the wound is in the proliferative phase?
options: A fibrin clot is sealing the edges of the wound.
The scar is becoming flatter and paler.
Red, moist granulation tissue is filling the base of the wound.
The wound is warm and swollen, as it was on the first day.
questions.rationale:
In the proliferative (granulation) phase, from about days 5 to 7, fibroblasts lay down new collagen, new blood vessels grow, and red, moist granulation tissue fills the wound from the base, while new epithelium spreads from the edges. Wound contraction plays a larger part in wounds that heal by secondary intention.

A fibrin clot forms during hemostasis, right after the injury. A scar that becomes flatter and paler is part of maturation, which starts around week 3 and lasts up to a year. Warmth and swelling in the first days reflect the inflammatory phase.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing burns on several clients. For each finding, click to specify the depth of the burn.
rows: Extends through the skin into muscle and bone
Dry and leathery, does not blanch, with eschar present
Moist, weeping blisters that are very painful and blanch with pressure
Red, dry, and painful, with no blisters; blanches with pressure
questions.rationale: A superficial (first-degree) burn involves only the epidermis: it is red, dry, painful, and blanches, without blisters, and usually heals without scarring. A partial-thickness (second-degree) burn involves the epidermis and part of the dermis: superficial partial-thickness burns form blisters, weep, are very painful, and blanch, while deep partial-thickness burns are mottled and don't blanch. A full-thickness (third-degree) burn extends through the whole dermis, often into the subcutaneous tissue: it is dry and leathery, doesn't blanch, and may have eschar (dead dermis). A fourth-degree burn extends beyond the skin into muscle, nerves, tendons, or bone.

questions.stem: An adult client has partial-thickness burns over the entire right arm and the entire front of the trunk. Using the rule of nines, what percentage of the total body surface area (TBSA) is burned?
questions.rationale:
In the adult rule of nines, each arm (upper extremity) is 9% and the front of the trunk is 18%: 9% + 18% = 27%.

The other values are 9% for the head and neck, 18% for the back of the trunk, 18% for each leg, and 1% for the perineum, which add up to 100%.

questions.stem: An adult client has burns over the entire left leg and the perineum. Using the rule of nines, what percentage of the total body surface area is burned?
questions.rationale:
In the adult rule of nines, each leg (lower extremity, front and back) is 18% and the perineum is 1%: 18% + 1% = 19%.

Each arm is 9%, the head and neck are 9%, and the front and the back of the trunk are 18% each.

questions.stem: An adult has several small burns scattered over both legs. The nurse estimates their total size using the client's palm. About how much of the total body surface area does the client's palm represent?
questions.rationale:
The client's own palm is about 1% of the total body surface area, which makes it useful for estimating small or scattered burns that are hard to measure with the rule of nines.

9% is the value for one arm, or for the head and neck, in the rule of nines, and 18% is the value for one leg, or for the front or the back of the trunk. 5% is not a value in either method.

questions.stem: Which adult burn injury is classified as a major burn that is best managed in a burn center?
options: A partial-thickness burn covering 10% of the total body surface area, on the back
A partial-thickness burn covering 17% of the total body surface area, on the trunk
A full-thickness burn covering 12% of the total body surface area
A full-thickness burn covering 5% of the total body surface area, on the thigh
questions.rationale:
A major burn in an adult covers more than 25% of the TBSA, includes a full-thickness burn of more than 10%, or involves the face, perineum, or extremities. Major burns are best managed in a burn center.

A partial-thickness burn of less than 15% that doesn't involve the face or perineum is a minor burn, usually managed as an outpatient. A partial-thickness burn of 15% to 20%, or a full-thickness burn of 2% to 10%, is a moderate burn that needs admission but not always a burn center.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who has large burns. Which complications should the nurse monitor for?
options: Increased sweating from the burned skin
Improved sensation in the burned area
Hypothermia
Fluid loss and dehydration
Infection and sepsis
questions.rationale:
Burns destroy the skin's barrier, so the body loses fluid through the wound, which can lead to dehydration, and microorganisms can enter, leading to infection and sepsis. Losing skin also impairs temperature regulation, so the client is at risk for hypothermia.

Deep burns destroy the sweat glands, so sweating does not increase in burned skin. Deep burns also destroy nerve endings, which reduces sensation in the area rather than improving it.

questions.stem: A client arrives at the emergency department with a small burn on the hand after touching a live electrical wire. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options: A small skin burn means the injury is minor.
The damage under the skin can be much more extensive than the burn on the surface.
Electrical injuries damage only the skin where the wire touched it.
Electrical burns are the most common reason for burn center admission.
questions.rationale:
Electrical injuries can cause deep tissue damage and complications in many body systems, so a small mark on the skin doesn't show the full injury. How severe it is depends on the voltage, the type of current, the body's resistance, and how long the contact lasted.

A small skin burn doesn't mean the injury is minor, and the damage is not limited to the skin. Thermal burns, from hot surfaces, liquids, steam, or flame, are the most common cause of burn center admission (about 86%), not electrical burns.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing pressure injuries on several clients. For each finding, click to specify the stage.
rows: A blister or shallow open sore that does not go through the full thickness of the skin
A deep crater that reaches muscle, tendon, or bone
Intact skin with a reddened area that does not blanch when pressed
A crater that extends below the skin into the fatty tissue
questions.rationale: A stage 1 pressure injury is intact skin with redness that doesn't blanch; in darker skin, the area may look red, purple, or blue and be harder to see, and it may feel warm or cool and firm. Stage 2 is a blister or shallow open sore that doesn't go through the full thickness of the skin. At stage 3, the sore becomes a crater below the skin surface, into the fat. At stage 4, the crater deepens to muscle, bone, tendon, or joint.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing a pressure injury risk assessment. Which client factors increase the risk?
options: Skin that is often damp from incontinence
Walking in the hallway several times a day
Staying in one position for long periods
Drinking enough fluids and eating protein-rich foods
Decreased sensation in the legs
Eating less than half of each meal
questions.rationale:
Pressure injuries form when prolonged pressure reduces blood flow to tissue, especially over bony prominences. Immobility keeps pressure on the same areas, moisture softens the skin and makes it easier to damage, poor nutrition weakens the skin and slows healing, and decreased sensation means the client doesn't feel the discomfort that normally prompts a change of position.

Walking several times a day relieves pressure, and good hydration and protein intake support skin integrity, so both lower the risk.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that increase the client's risk for pressure injuries.
questions.passage: Client is [[alert and oriented]]. Reports right hip pain and [[prefers to stay on the back, because turning hurts]]. [[Has eaten about one-quarter of each meal for 2 days]]. [[Was incontinent of urine overnight; the sheets were damp at 0600]]. [[Skin over the sacrum is intact]]. Client has [[type 2 diabetes mellitus]] and [[reports decreased feeling in both feet]].
questions.rationale:
The risk factors are staying in one position (immobility from pain), eating about one-quarter of meals (poor nutrition), damp sheets after incontinence (moisture), diabetes (which impairs circulation and healing), and decreased feeling in the feet (the client may not feel the discomfort of pressure).

Being alert and oriented isn't a risk factor: the client can report discomfort and take part in care. Intact skin over the sacrum is a normal finding to keep checking, not a risk factor.

questions.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether it is indicated or not indicated for the client.
rows: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours
Place a pillow under the calves so the heels float off the bed
Massage the reddened area on the right heel
Clean and dry the skin promptly after each incontinence episode
Encourage protein-rich foods and fluids
Let the client stay on the back to avoid hip pain
questions.rationale:
Repositioning at least every 2 hours and floating the heels on a pillow under the calves relieve pressure on the skin. Cleaning and drying the skin after incontinence removes moisture that softens the skin. Protein and fluids support skin integrity and healing, and the client has been eating and drinking little.

Massaging a reddened area over a bony prominence is not indicated, because rubbing can further damage the fragile tissue. Letting the client stay on the back keeps pressure on the heels and sacrum; the nurse should manage the pain, for example by offering prescribed pain medication before turning, and still reposition the client.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the client's findings at 0800.

options: Cellulitis of the heel
Stage 1 pressure injury
Full-thickness burn
Stage 2 pressure injury
Keep the client on the back to limit hip pain
Encourage protein-rich foods and fluids
Apply a heating pad to the heel
Massage the heel to restore blood flow
Relieve pressure on the heel by repositioning and floating it
Color and blanching of the area on the right heel
Visual acuity
Food and fluid intake
Hearing in each ear
Bowel sounds

questions.rationale:
Intact skin with a dark red area that doesn't blanch over a bony prominence is a stage 1 pressure injury. It isn't stage 2, because there is no blister or open area. Cellulitis would show spreading redness, warmth, swelling, and pain, often with a fever and a raised white blood cell count, which the client doesn't have. There is no history of a burn.

The nurse should relieve pressure on the heel by repositioning the client and floating the heel, and support nutrition and hydration, since the client is eating and drinking little and the albumin is low. Massage can further damage the tissue, a heating pad can burn skin with reduced sensation, and staying on the back keeps pressure on the heels.

To see whether the plan is working, the nurse monitors the color and blanching of the heel and the client's food and fluid intake. Visual acuity, bowel sounds, and hearing don't show the response to this care.

questions.stem: At 1600, the nurse finds that the area on the right heel has opened into a shallow sore. The redness around it has spread, the skin is warmer, there is cloudy yellow drainage, and the client's temperature is 38.4° C (101.1° F). Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Record the findings and recheck the heel at the end of the shift.
Cover the heel and wait to see whether the fever goes away.
Report the wound changes and the fever to the provider.
Ask the client to walk to improve circulation to the heel.
questions.rationale:
Spreading redness, more warmth, cloudy drainage, and a new fever suggest that the wound has become infected, and the open sore means the injury has progressed to stage 2. These are significant changes, and the nurse should report them promptly to the provider, using a structured format such as SBAR, so treatment can begin.

Waiting until the end of the shift or waiting for the fever to go away delays care for a possible infection. Covering the wound is part of care, but it doesn't replace reporting the change. Asking a client who had hip surgery 3 days ago to walk on a painful heel doesn't treat the infection and may be unsafe.

questions.stem: A nurse notes a shiny, pink, pearly bump with tiny visible blood vessels on a client's nose. The nurse recognizes this as a common sign of which skin cancer?
options: Melanoma
Squamous cell carcinoma
Seborrheic dermatitis
Basal cell carcinoma
questions.rationale:
Basal cell carcinoma, the most common skin cancer, typically looks like a shiny, pink or skin-colored bump with telangiectasia (small visible blood vessels). It rarely spreads, but it can destroy the tissue around it, especially on the face and ears, so early treatment matters.

Melanoma, the most lethal skin cancer, arises from melanocytes and usually shows the ABCDE changes in a pigmented spot. Squamous cell carcinoma, the second most common, appears as a scaly, red or darker bump or patch. Seborrheic dermatitis isn't a cancer: it causes red patches with a yellowish scale, such as dandruff.

questions.stem: A client asks a nurse which changes in a mole should be checked by a provider. Which findings should the nurse include?
options: The mole is round, evenly brown, and 3 mm across.
The mole has several shades of brown and black.
The mole has changed in size, shape, or color.
The mole is larger than 6 mm across.
One half of the mole doesn't match the other half.
The border is ragged, notched, or blurred.
questions.rationale:
The ABCDE warning signs of melanoma are Asymmetry (the halves don't match), an irregular Border (ragged, notched, or blurred), uneven Color (several shades), a Diameter larger than 6 mm, and Evolving (changes in size, shape, or color). Any of these should be checked.

A round, evenly colored mole smaller than 6 mm shows none of the warning signs, though the client should still watch it for changes.

questions.stem: For each skin condition, click to specify what causes it.
rows: Grouped blisters on a red base on the lip (a cold sore)
A painful, blistering rash in a band on one side of the body, in a client who had chickenpox as a child
Intensely itchy papules that are worse at night and spread by skin-to-skin contact
Cracked, itchy skin with small blisters between the toes
questions.rationale: A cold sore is caused by herpes simplex virus type 1, which stays in the body and can reactivate. Shingles (herpes zoster) is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, which lies dormant in the sensory ganglia after chickenpox and can reactivate years later, causing a painful rash along one dermatome. Scabies is caused by a mite that burrows into the skin and causes intense itching, worse at night; it spreads by close skin-to-skin contact. Athlete's foot (tinea pedis) is a fungal infection.

questions.stem: A client has itchy, red, oozing patches on both forearms after clearing poison ivy from a yard. Which teaching is the most important part of the client's treatment?
options: Avoid touching the plant or substance that caused the reaction.
Cover the patches with a tight bandage that doesn't let air in.
Expect the rash itself to spread to other people by touch.
Apply an antifungal cream to the patches twice a day.
questions.rationale:
This is contact dermatitis: itchy, red, oozing lesions where the skin touched an irritant or allergen, here poison ivy. The most important part of treatment is to identify the cause and avoid it. An antihistamine or a hydrocortisone cream may be prescribed for the reaction.

A tight bandage traps moisture and doesn't treat the cause. Contact dermatitis is a reaction, not an infection, so the rash itself doesn't spread from person to person, although plant oil left on the skin or clothes can cause new reactions. An antifungal cream treats fungal infections, not contact dermatitis.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about skin changes during pregnancy.
questions.text: Pink to silvery lines on the abdomen from rapid stretching of the skin are called {{0}}. Brown patches on the cheeks and forehead that darken with sun exposure are called {{1}}. A dark line down the middle of the abdomen is called the {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
Striae gravidarum are the stretch marks of pregnancy: linear scars that form when the skin stretches quickly and the connective tissue of the dermis is disrupted. Melasma (chloasma) is darkening of sun-exposed areas of the face, influenced by hormones and UV light. The linea nigra is a darker line down the center of the abdomen.

Vitiligo is a loss of skin pigment, not darkening. Acanthosis nigricans is dark, velvety skin in body folds, associated with insulin resistance.

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis of the liver has pitting edema in both legs. Which mechanism explains the edema?
options: The capillaries become more permeable, as they do after a severe burn.
The lymphatic vessels are blocked, so fluid can't drain from the tissues.
Less albumin is made, so oncotic pressure falls and fluid leaves the vessels.
A clot in a deep leg vein raises the pressure in that leg's capillaries.
questions.rationale:
The liver makes albumin, the main protein that keeps fluid in the blood vessels (oncotic pressure). In liver failure or cirrhosis, less protein is made, oncotic pressure falls, and fluid moves out of the capillaries into the tissues, causing edema in both legs.

Increased capillary permeability causes edema with burns, insect bites, cellulitis, and allergic reactions. Lymphatic obstruction occurs with conditions such as cancer, surgery, or filariasis. A deep vein thrombosis raises the hydrostatic pressure in one leg's capillaries, so the edema is usually on one side only.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client who is starting a medication given by transdermal patch. Which advantages of the patch should the nurse include?
options: It avoids first-pass metabolism by the liver.
It delivers the medication steadily over time.
It can deliver large doses of any medication.
It works best when applied over irritated skin.
It bypasses the stomach and intestines.
questions.rationale:
A transdermal patch gives continuous, steady delivery through the skin into the bloodstream. It bypasses the gastrointestinal tract, which avoids stomach irritation, and it avoids the first-pass metabolism in the liver that affects oral drugs. Patches can also make it easier for clients to take their medication as prescribed.

Patches go on healthy, intact skin, because irritated or damaged skin changes how much drug is absorbed. Only drugs with small molecules and a low daily dose work in a patch, so a patch can't deliver large doses of any medication.

questions.stem: Which instruction should a nurse give a client about applying a transdermal patch?
options: Apply a moisturizing lotion first so the patch sticks better.
Wash the site with plain water, dry it well, and rotate sites.
Put each new patch on the same spot so the dose stays the same.
Place the patch over an area of irritated skin to soothe it.
questions.rationale:
The client should clean the site with plain water, pat it completely dry, and rotate sites with each new patch to avoid skin irritation. Some patches are worn for part of a day, and others for several days, such as a fentanyl patch worn for 72 hours.

Soaps, alcohol, lotions, and oils should not be used just before applying a patch, because they can keep it from sticking and change absorption. Using the same spot every time irritates the skin. A patch shouldn't go on irritated or damaged skin, which changes how much medication is absorbed.

questions.stem: A nurse is performing a skin assessment. For each finding, click to specify the technique the nurse uses to assess it.
rows: Color
Temperature
Texture
Turgor
Distribution of a rash
questions.rationale: The skin assessment uses inspection and palpation. The nurse inspects (looks at) the color of the skin and the distribution of a rash or lesions. The nurse palpates (touches) to assess temperature, with the back of the hand, texture, and turgor (how quickly lifted skin returns to place). Moisture can be both seen and felt.

questions.stem: For each client, click to specify the transmission-based precautions the nurse should use, in addition to standard precautions.
rows: A client with a draining wound infected with MRSA
A client with influenza
A client with active pulmonary tuberculosis
A client with scabies
questions.rationale: Contact precautions (gloves and a gown on entering the room, and hand hygiene on leaving) are used for infections spread by direct or indirect contact, such as an MRSA wound and scabies. Droplet precautions (a surgical mask within 3 to 6 feet of the client) are used for infections spread by large respiratory droplets, such as influenza. Airborne precautions (a negative-pressure room and an N95 respirator) are used for infections spread by tiny particles that stay in the air, such as tuberculosis.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to assess a client's skin, including a draining wound. Which actions follow standard precautions?
options: Wear gloves only if the client looks ill.
Wear gloves when touching the wound or its drainage.
Perform hand hygiene before and after the assessment.
Keep the same gloves on to assess the next client.
Discard the soiled dressing in the proper container.
questions.rationale:
Standard precautions apply to every client: hand hygiene before and after contact, gloves when touching broken skin, mucous membranes, or body fluids such as wound drainage, and proper disposal of contaminated materials. A gown is added if drainage could splash.

Gloves are chosen for the task (contact with drainage or broken skin), not for how ill the client looks. Gloves are never kept on between clients, because that carries microorganisms from one client to the next.

questions.stem: A client who prefers to speak Haitian Creole is having a skin assessment, and the nurse needs to ask about a new rash and itching. Which action is best?
options: Use a qualified medical interpreter for the health history.
Ask the client's teenage daughter to interpret.
Speak slowly and loudly in English.
Skip the history and do only the physical examination.
questions.rationale:
A qualified medical interpreter makes sure the client understands the questions and can describe the symptoms accurately and privately. That supports an accurate assessment, the client's own decisions about care, and the client's dignity.

A family member, especially a child, may not translate medical terms correctly and limits the client's privacy. Speaking slowly and loudly in English doesn't overcome a language barrier. Skipping the history leaves out key information, such as when the rash started and what makes it itch.
